blocks.text: The opening portrays the heavens as continuously declaring God's glory, though they use no ordinary audible language. Later, the psalm describes the LORD's judgments through images of both value and pleasure: they are more desirable than fine gold and sweeter than honey. They do more than delight, however; they also warn the servant.

One way of reading the poem's structure is to see a turn from creation's testimony to the LORD's instruction. Verses 7-11 name that instruction in several ways—law, testimony, precepts, commandment, fear, and ordinances—before the speaker examines his own conduct. His prayer distinguishes hidden faults, which he cannot discern, from presumptuous sins, which are deliberate and self-asserting.

The sun is compared first to a bridegroom emerging from his chamber and then to a strong runner rejoicing to complete a course. Together, the similes emphasize joy, strength, and comprehensive reach. The closing prayer then shifts attention to the speaker's own words and inward meditation, asking that both be acceptable to the LORD, whom he calls his rock and redeemer.
